name: Cottage Village
description: In a village, there are `n` non-overlapping square houses with their centers on the Ox-axis. Given their center coordinates and side lengths, determine how many possible positions exist for a new square house of a given side `t`. The new house must also be centered on the Ox-axis, touch at least one existing house, and not overlap any.

input_spec.line_1: Two space-separated integers: `n` (number of existing houses) and `t` (side length of the new house).
input_spec.lines_2_to_n+1: Each of the next `n` lines contains two space-separated integers: `xi` (x-coordinate of the center of a house) and `ai` (its side length).

output_spec.description: A single integer representing the total count of possible positions for the new house.

notes: A house with center `(xi, 0)` and side `ai` occupies the x-interval `[xi - ai/2, xi + ai/2]`.
The problem can be solved by first sorting the houses by their x-coordinates.
There are always two unique positions available at the two ends of the sorted row of houses.
For each gap between two adjacent houses, there can be 0, 1, or 2 additional positions depending on how the new house of side `t` fits into the gap.
If the gap is larger than `t`, there are 2 new positions. If the gap is exactly `t`, there is 1 new position. If the gap is smaller than `t`, there are 0 new positions.
To avoid floating-point arithmetic with `ai/2`, it is advisable to work with doubled coordinates.

examples.explanation: The two houses are at [-2, 2] and [5, 7]. The gap between them is 3 units wide. A house of side 2 fits with space to spare, creating two positions in the gap. Adding the two positions at the ends gives a total of 4.
The houses are at [-2, 2] and [4, 6]. The gap is exactly 2 units. A house of side 2 fits perfectly, touching both, creating one position. Adding the two end positions gives a total of 3.
The houses are at [-2, 2] and [4, 6]. The gap is 2 units. A house of side 3 cannot fit. Only the two positions at the ends of the village are possible.

examples.title: Problem Example 1: Gap Larger Than House
examples.why_included: This is the first example from the problem statement. The gap between houses is larger than the new house, allowing two positions.

examples.title: Problem Example 2: Gap Equals House Size
examples.why_included: This is the second example. The gap is exactly the size of the new house, allowing one position.

examples.title: Problem Example 3: Gap Smaller Than House
examples.why_included: This is the third example. The gap is too small for the new house, allowing zero positions within the gap.

examples.title: Minimum N: Single Existing House
examples.why_included: Tests the minimum `n=1` constraint. With only one house, there are no gaps, so there are always exactly two possible positions.

examples.title: Unsorted Input Houses Test
examples.why_included: The input houses are not sorted by their x-coordinate. A correct solution must sort them first before calculating gaps.

examples.title: All Gaps Larger Than House Size
examples.why_included: A straightforward case where every gap between houses is large, each contributing two positions. Total = 2 (ends) + 2 * (n-1).

examples.title: All Gaps Equal to House Size
examples.why_included: A case where every gap is exactly the size of the new house, each contributing one position. Total = 2 (ends) + (n-1).

examples.title: All Gaps Smaller Than House Size
examples.why_included: A case where no gap is large enough, so only the two positions at the ends are possible.

examples.title: All Houses Touching, Zero Gaps
examples.why_included: Tests the edge case where all houses touch, meaning all gaps are of size zero. The answer must be 2.

examples.title: Mix of Different Gap Types
examples.why_included: A general case with a mix of gaps: one equal to house size, and two smaller. This tests the conditional logic thoroughly.

examples.title: Houses at Negative Coordinates
examples.why_included: Ensures the solution works correctly when house centers are at negative x-coordinates.

examples.title: Houses Straddling Zero Coordinate
examples.why_included: Tests a mix of negative and positive coordinates, including one centered near zero.

examples.title: Parity Check: Gap is 2t-1
examples.why_included: Creates a gap one unit smaller than the house requires. Using floating point math might fail here, but integer-based logic (doubling coordinates) is robust.

examples.title: Parity Check: Gap is 2t+1
examples.why_included: Creates a gap one unit larger than the house requires. Tests off-by-one logic for the '>' comparison.

examples.title: Houses With Same Side Length as New House
examples.why_included: A specific case where all existing houses and the new house have the same side length.

examples.title: Maximum Number of Houses, Large Gaps
examples.why_included: A stress test with the maximum number of houses, all spaced far apart. This tests the performance of the sorting and iteration. The answer is 2 + 2 * 999.

examples.title: Maximum Number of Touching Houses
examples.why_included: Stress test with max `n`. All houses are touching, leaving zero-sized gaps. The new house is large, so only the two end positions are valid.
